beats.narration_text: Selam. This is Jainil. Two services. The one that produces the data validates what it sends. The one that consumes it validates what it receives. Both sets of tests are green, both have been green all week, and the numbers downstream are still wrong. This is not a rare situation and it is not anybody being careless. It is a gap in where the checks are placed.

show.event: composer on cream, spark + 'Selam, Jainil' above it
the question types itself in
send arms terracotta, running indicator
two output lines land

props.command: Both services validate their data and both pass. The output is still wrong. How?
output: Nothing checks the join between them.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. A record can be perfectly valid on the way out and perfectly valid on the way in, and still mean something different at each end. Validation inside a stage cannot see that. Only a check between the stages can.

show.event: empty cream page, caret blinking
writer types 'The data was validated on both sides.'
writer stops on 'sides', deletes it
'sides, but never between them' types in its place

props.text:
The data was validated
on both sides.

beats.narration_text: Here is the shape of it. The producer emits five thousand payment events and checks its own output: every field present, every type right, every timestamp positive. The consumer receives them and runs the same kind of check on its input. Both pass. And in between those two boxes there is a place where nobody has put anything at all, because it belongs to neither team.

show.event: the producer card springs up
arrow draws, the empty middle card lands and fills terracotta
arrow draws, the consumer card lands
the terracotta note under the middle: nobody owns this

props.title: WHERE THE CHECKS ACTUALLY SIT
props.caption: Both stages are well tested. The gap is between them.

beats.narration_text: So I took a clean batch and broke it seven ways — all ordinary integration failures. Timestamps in seconds instead of milliseconds. Amounts in cents instead of dollars. A new status value nobody announced. Nulls written as minus one. A timezone shift. Amounts arriving as strings. Late rows duplicating an id. Each stage's own checks caught exactly one of the seven: the string, because that is the only one that changes a type. A contract at the boundary caught six.

show.event: title, then the first bar grows — barely off the floor at 1
the boundary bar grows to 6
the last bar reaches 7 and lights terracotta
caption lands

props.title: DEFECTS CAUGHT, OUT OF SEVEN
props.caption: Seven ordinary integration failures, each applied on its own.

beats.narration_text: The seventh is the interesting one. A timezone shift of five and a half hours. Against an epoch timestamp in milliseconds that is a change of about one thousandth of one percent — far inside any range check you would write. So the boundary contract waved it through. But the events have a daily rhythm, quiet overnight and busy in the afternoon, and shifting everything by five hours moves that shape a long way. Profile the distribution instead of the median, and it is obvious.

show.event: the first card lands — what a range check sees
the second card lands — what a shape check sees
the second card's terracotta heading makes the contrast

cards.title: a shape check sees
lines: verdict: this is not the same data

props.title: THE ONE THAT GOT THROUGH
props.caption: Same defect. The difference is which quantity you agreed to watch.

beats.narration_text: This is not a niche concern. Google built a production system for exactly this problem and described it in twenty nineteen: validation that sits in the pipeline and checks each batch of data, rather than tests that sit inside one service. It runs inside their machine learning platform across a very large amount of production data.

show.event: cream card, the reference lines reveal as the voice reaches them
citation settles beneath, smaller and softer

lines: A production data-validation system at Google, deployed inside their TFX machine-learning platform.
It detects anomalies in the data fed into pipelines — including training and serving drifting apart.
meta: REFERENCE (paraphrased, not quoted) — Breck, Zinkevich, Polyzotis, Whang & Roy, “Data Validation for Machine Learning”, SysML 2019

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Point this at a handoff you actually own: here are two services that exchange data — help me write down the contract between them as a set of checks on a batch, not on a row, including the ranges, the allowed values, the key uniqueness and the shape of the distribution. The last of those is the one most people leave out.
